blocks.1: These are thoughts that have come to me while gathering and writing down what is printed above.
blocks.2: The village lies beautiful and sheltered, and from the very earliest times people have enjoyed, and benefited from, its fortunate position. Of all the sheltered inlets (gavlar) here in Gaulom, this one was chosen as a gathering place because it was so conveniently placed. Here, sheltered by islands and hills, they found the ideal place for their religious gatherings. Here they met for sacrifices and sacrificial feasts; here they had their sanctuaries. Its favourable, and not least central, position meant that people from an ever larger area met here. They liked it here and found good conditions for their gatherings. The large, shady oaks below the slope and the rock face, sheltered from the sea breeze, were as if made for a sacrificial grove, and the rise to the south was very well suited as a place for the sacrificial rites.
blocks.3: The priest of the sacrifices (offergode), who looked after the sanctuaries and led the sacrifices and the religious ceremonies, gradually became an important person. He saw to it that everything was made ready for the feast and organised the large gatherings. He came into contact with many powerful and respected men, who often stayed with him in the period around the gatherings. They discussed various problems among themselves and sought each other's advice. Many tangles were often resolved in the conversations at such gatherings in connection with the sacrificial feasts. But it surely took a long time before settling matters by fist and violence came completely to an end. Duels (holmgang) were often fought on Timmerøya. Later this island was used as a place of execution and a burial place for the executed and for people who took their own lives.
blocks.4: As time went on, more and more disputes were settled by the opposing parties each appointing their own men to decide how the dispute should be resolved. The way cases were decided created norms for how various disputes should be settled, and little by little rules were shaped and established that were used more and more commonly, and which at last were generally accepted as guidelines and customs in everyday life. In addition to being a religious gathering place, the place by the temple and sacrificial grove also became a place where rules were discussed and shaped into laws, and, in time, decisions in the form of judgements were made. The activity grew, and more and more people, from ever larger areas, came here to have their cases decided peacefully. The rules of life shaped here became more and more widely known, respected and accepted as laws.
blocks.5: More and more people came together at the gatherings here in the inlet at the mouth of the ravine, or gjøli, as they said. People who came from outside simply called the place Gjøli, which then became Guli. At the approach a staff, a marker, was set up to show that they were now rowing into holy ground. The headland where the marker stood was called Stafneset.
blocks.6: The gatherings in Guli kept developing; they grew larger and larger and more and more important. The legal activity gradually became well known and extensive, and the number of cases became so great that it became an institution of its own, the assembly system. In time the laws also became so many that it was hard to keep track of them all. Persons were then chosen who had special responsibility for learning the laws and remembering them. These men were called law-speakers. The gatherings developed so that the assembly sessions became the most extensive, but the religious gatherings were still of great value to the people. The lawman became the most important person at the assemblies; he presided over the assembly and saw to it that the assembly peace prevailed as long as the session lasted.
blocks.7: More and more people came to the assemblies. The number of judges increased, the parties to cases brought advisers with them, and many witnesses came forward. In addition many came just to meet kinsmen and friends. Some came to trade, to get jewellery and valuable everyday things.
blocks.8: The assembly field was marked off with hazel poles below the slope up towards the ravine, sheltered by large, leafy oaks. The people who gathered on the terraces of the slope had a good view of the assembly site and could easily hear what went on. In the earliest times most things took place under the open sky, but in time hide tents were put up, and later assembly booths.
blocks.9: Western Norway was probably the most important region of Norway in the early saga age. There was a great deal of contact with the outside world across the seas here, and it was probably here that the most powerful chieftains lived. This therefore became the most valuable part of the kingdom for the king when Harald Fairhair united the country into one kingdom. He came early into contact with the men of the old Gulating and made use of the legal system established here. He made the institution the assembly for a large area, and the Gulating law gained an important role. The guidelines and fundamental ideas of the law were carried on in Magnus the Lawmender's national law of 1274 and, through Christian V's law of 1687, in fact partly right up to our Constitution of 1814.
blocks.10: Here in Guli the traffic grew ever livelier. The old religious feasts continued, and the assembly system became a large organisation, whose district at its greatest covered the whole of Western Norway from Sunnmøre in the north to the Agder counties in the south. In addition Valdres, Hallingdal and Setesdal belonged to it, and all the North Sea islands and Iceland until they got their own assemblies.
blocks.11: In spring great fleets of Viking ships made for Guli. Many people came, and they had large stores of food and mead. On top of that came the goods they were to barter and trade. The assembly travellers were summoned to Stemnebø. Here watchmen were stationed who checked the boats, and dramatic situations could surely arise. Sometimes people were killed here if they resisted the watchmen's orders. In larger conflicts the guards called for help from the watch booths on the slope by the river above. The island outside was given the name Dragarøya by the assembly travellers. This was because when they came there they had to draw down the sail to be inspected by the guards. People who lived in the area later called the island Segløya, but the name “Dragerøen” was commonly used by people outside the district until well into our own time.
blocks.12: The priest of the sacrifices, in addition to looking after the old sanctuaries, was also given responsibility for keeping the assembly site, and what belonged to it, ready for use. He also commanded the watch and had many helpers and a large guard in his service. It became a large household, both at Stemnebø and in Guli, so it was useful that he had large properties both on the mainland and on many of the islands outside. There was plenty of fish and herring in the sounds and fjords, and in addition to farming there was hunting and fishing both summer and winter. He had the best farmland east of the assembly site, along and at the head of the large bay there. On the slopes and along the river at the bottom of the valley there was plenty of game. The soil was fertile, and many good plots of land and fine farmsteads had been cleared here. Out along the sounds there were also large areas of good soil, sheltered coves and many fine farmsteads.
blocks.13: After Harald Fairhair had conquered the country, great changes came about here. It was then that the assembly system in Guli became truly known far and wide and came to mean so much for the shaping of the legal system in the country. The Gulating law became known for its good, democratic construction and its solid roots in the people. Since then it has been said, as strongly as this, that “the cradle of democracy in Norway stood in Gulen.”
blocks.14: The king became an important person at the Gulating, as at the other assemblies in our country. He used the assembly to achieve his aims in governing the country, and as time went on it was he who had the assembly summoned, and he gained great influence over the decisions. Here we may think of what happened at the assembly site the day Eirik Bloodaxe and Queen Gunnhild arranged things so that Berg-Onund won the inheritance case against Egil Skallagrimsson. We picture the tall, coarse, strong, somewhat shaggy Egil, after consulting Arinbjørn, running in anger with his men through Monsverket and the grove, over the ridge and down to a cove further out, where the rest of his men lay with the ships ready to leave. They quickly got aboard and rowed at full speed north through Nyhamarsundet together with his kinsman Arinbjørn and his men, who followed. Further, we see Queen Gunnhild egging on the king and his men to go after Egil, and how the king's men rowed flat out along Prestesundet, headed north and saw Arinbjørn's ships in “Saudungssund”.
blocks.15: There were surely many other exciting events here too – if only we could look back!
blocks.16: In the earliest times the people gathered for sacrifices at a collection of stones set up in fixed formations, a “horg” (stone altar). The blood of the sacrificial animals was sprinkled over the stones, the fuel for the fire and the people, before the fire where the sacrifice took place was lit. Sometimes humans were also sacrificed.
blocks.17: The sacrificial blood, the laut, was kept in blood bowls, and blood twigs were used to sprinkle it about. After the sacrifice the meat of the sacrificial animals was boiled in large cauldrons and a feast was held. The meat of the sacrificial animals was eaten to come into contact with the divine powers. There were three main annual sacrifices: at winter nights, 14 October; at midwinter; and at the first day of summer, 14 April.
blocks.18: On the rise south-east of the assembly site, where the large horg stood, a spacious temple (hov) was built, in which the sacred objects were placed and where the sacrificial ceremonies then took place. The priest of the sacrifices was given responsibility for the temple and was now called the temple priest (hovgode). The slaughter of the sacrificial animals still took place in the sacrificial grove, and the sacrificial vessels were washed in water from the holy sacrificial spring as before. The temple was divided into three parts: the entrance, like a porch, then a large room called the peace room, and innermost a choir with an altar and a panel with images of the gods. On the altar lay a gold ring on which they laid their hands when they swore oaths. At all gatherings the temple priest wore the ring on one hand. The blood bowl with the blood twig in it stood by the altar. The meat of the sacrificial animals was now boiled over fires along the floor of the temple. The people sat round the fires with the cauldrons of meat. It was like a great banquet. In addition to plenty of good food there was, as usual at great feasts, also plenty of good drink. The temple priest carried filled drinking horns among the farmers and dedicated the drink to the honour of the gods.
blocks.19: First they drank Odin's horn for victory and power. Those who trusted most in their own power and strength silently dedicated the horn to Thor. Then followed Njord's horn, and then the horn to Freyr. These were emptied for good harvests and for peace. Then they drank Bragi's horn, at which solemn vows were made, and then came the memorial toast for departed kinsmen.
blocks.20: The biggest matter ever discussed at the Gulating, and the one that led to the greatest upheaval for the place here and for the whole country, was surely the introduction of Christianity. Several of our kings had gone on raids as Viking kings and had come to know the new faith abroad. Even before the kings tried to introduce the Christian faith, missionaries from other countries in Europe had been here. The temple priest had several times had visits from people who wanted to win him for the new faith and in that way make it easier to get the faith accepted among the people. The first king who made a real attempt to introduce Christianity, Håkon the Good, grew up in England and came to know the faith there. He was influenced by the ideas of Glastonbury Abbey, which was one of England's most important spiritual centres at the time.
blocks.21: In the time the Fairhair dynasty had been kings in the country, the religious ceremonies had little by little been shaped according to new norms. But the old Norse faith was deeply rooted in the people here, as in other parts of the country, and they found it hard to give up the rites, and discard the symbols, that through generations had been used to win the favour and protection of the old gods. People were afraid of bringing down the wrath of the Æsir and took many of the old customs with them into life under the new faith. When the young Håkon Adalsteinsfostre tried to clear away the old religious customs, the new faith was not yet properly accepted here. Many doubted the teaching he had brought from England. They found it safest to stick to the Æsir in many important matters. Håkon himself was a very good king, and the people gradually came to trust more and more that the powers he was connected with were the good forces. New Christian kings came, and little by little the new faith won out over the old Norse faith.
blocks.22: The temple was torn down. The sacrificial grove disappeared as the trees were cut down and partly burned. No one dared use the fine oaks; people were still afraid that it might bring the wrath of the gods upon them and that the Æsir might still take revenge on those who used the timber for worldly purposes. So the trees were left lying where they had been felled, and they lay so that, when leaves and rubbish floated against them, they formed a dam that became firmer and tighter as soil, and with it grass and bushes, made the dam stronger. This led the little pond where the small stream ran to grow larger and make the ground around it boggy.
blocks.23: The old sacrificial stones disappeared; the people lost their heathen sanctuaries.
blocks.24: Symbols to gather around meant a great deal to everyone, and the heathen signs were replaced by new Christian rallying points. The kings and their priests put up the stone crosses. The cross at Krossteigen showed the people at the assembly that the White Christ had won; he was the strongest, he was the one they could rely on. They proclaimed the assembly peace beneath the holy cross. The cross was also given a special position. The king ordered it to be set where the old god-marker stood, which showed where the shadow had to stop before the power of the sun at the winter solstice, and now the cross became a sign that it was the White Christ and his faith that ruled at the assembly, pushed back the darkness, shone forth like the sun and spread over the whole kingdom. Christ led those who would follow him out of darkness into an existence of sun, warmth and growth. The feast of the winter solstice was given a new content.
blocks.25: Down on the mound where the temple had stood, another cross was put up. At a great mass baptism there, in connection with an assembly session, a solid stone font was used that later stood next to the cross when it came. Here, over the ages, many people were baptised into the Christian faith.
blocks.26: On the very spot where the temple stood, a church was built. The first church was a small, very simple wooden church, raised on wooden posts. It had an earth floor, a porch and a small octagonal altar rail. The font was put into this church. In the font was a brass bowl that was later hammered out into an octagonal dish. The dish was decorated with grooves and clusters.
blocks.27: There were hardly any seats in the church; the people had to stand, and the church was very cold. The roof too was of wood, brown tarred boards, but the church was not constructed as a stave church. This church came so early that the people still feared the wrath of the Æsir. Many were sceptical of the church and tried to damage it by fire.
blocks.28: The strong chieftain in Virkesdal, Torstein, was very angry when he got an order from the king to come and help build the church. Torstein was haymaking at the time. He became so angry that he cut furrows into the ground so deep that they were visible for a long time. He ran into the forest and cut down a big tree. He took the log with him, laid it before the king and said that if this log was not used as a doorpost in the church, he would not lift another hand on the building. The king thought it a fine log, and it was hewn and used as a doorpost as Torstein wanted. But the king did not like Torstein having horsemeat for his provisions.
blocks.29: The great religious gatherings continued, but now on the basis of the new faith and under Christian auspices. The apostles from Europe had left their mark. The temple priest and many of his helpers were among the first to go over to the new faith, and he became a priest and helper to the priests and monks the king sent to look after the church's interests here. The temple priest's acceptance of the new faith made it easier for the people to slip over to Christianity. Little by little the new rituals came in and the old ones gave way, but many of the heathen customs lingered for a long time.
blocks.30: The monks had their home in a small monastery over on Kirkeneset. Properties were given to the monastery so that the monks would have enough income to carry out their work. Several of these properties had earlier been under the temple priest's control. The monks were enterprising and energetic people. They followed their daily ritual, and the whole time there were monks here they cooperated well with the priests on religious life. They held masses, and every spring and autumn they walked in procession between the two crosses. In spring, on 3 May, there was the feast of the Cross to pray for a blessing on the year's crops, and in autumn, on 14 September, there was a mass of thanksgiving. At Michaelmas, 29 September, they held a mass for St Michael on the lower part of Fløyfjellet, on the level ground where they had a good view towards the sea. In time the mountain took its name from this and was called Mikkelfjellet.
blocks.31: Religious gatherings arranged by the priests were also held. The cross on the mound where the temple had stood became an important gathering place. The church that had been destroyed was restored. At the assembly sessions the oath was sworn there. Now they swore the oath by calling on God instead of turning to Freyr and Njord as before. The monks had their own church in the monastery.
blocks.32: After a long period of flourishing, quieter times came to the place here. The teeming life died down little by little, both on the religious side and as regards the assemblies. Buildings and other installations, both of the religious and the legal community, were poorly maintained and fell more or less into disrepair. There was strife between several who wanted royal power in the country. Kings who gained power did not sit securely; they had to fight their rivals, and many lost the throne after a short time. In several ways it was a time of decline. The king often had to hold assemblies at short notice, and the assemblies were often set in market towns where the king mostly stayed. He then did not have to set out on journeys and expose himself to attack. The Frostating was often held in Nidaros, and the Gulating in Bjørgvin, the plain between the mountains. But when Håkon Håkonsson brought order to the royal power and became strong and unassailable, he also restored the legal system to its old forms. He governed the country well, and never have Norway's borders been as wide as under him. He rebuilt the church at the assembly site. It was so dilapidated that little of the building material could be used. He made the church much bigger, finer and more practical; indeed it became like a completely new building, beautiful as it lay there on the rise.
blocks.33: Guli again became the regular gathering place of the assembly, but the assembly had now lost much of its scope. The number of jurors had been greatly reduced, and many of the tasks and cases were settled in other ways. The lawman had long since become a royal official, and with few judges and helpers around him he settled most things together with the king. Compared with earlier, very few came to the assemblies. It was now the religious gatherings that drew most people, as it had been in the very first period when the assemblies here began, a long time back. Håkon found it practical to move the assemblies down to the new church. There was a small, oblong rocky knoll there that was ideally suited as a law rock and for presiding over the assembly, so there, by the new law rock, they fenced off a new assembly field with hazel poles. On the slope up towards the rock face below the church and the Olav cross with the font, there was plenty of room for the crowds that now came to the assembly. The spacious place where the assembly used to be held, and the terrace/mound where the law-speaker stood generation after generation beneath the holy cross, long lay as a protected spot, but in recent times it was taken into use as farmland. The cross was not moved. It was to stand where it had been set as a memorial to the introduction of Christianity at the assembly, and as the Christian symbol of light's victory over darkness. The old assembly booths were restored; the king's booth became large and splendid.
blocks.34: The old sacrificial spring kept its holy status after the introduction of the Christian faith too. St Olav praised the clear, good water there. He and his men drank from the spring; they felt the water gave them new strength. The spring was later dedicated to St Olav, and it became usual for people to seek healing in the water.
blocks.35: The religious activity in the bay here flourished for a while longer, but the legal activity declined. The assemblies became rarer and rarer, and after a time they ceased altogether; all legal matters for our part of the country were dealt with in Bjørgvin.
blocks.36: The name Guli, which had become a name for the whole area here, went more and more out of use. Those who lived here used the local place names. Travellers from afar became few, and the local names came more and more to the fore. The bay here was referred to as the bay with the plain and the fields where the assembly stood, where the oath was sworn. People in the nearby areas often said the bay inside the islands. Here, as in many places, place names have changed over time, and after a long time the name became Eivindvik. People who lived further away, outside the district, still used the name Guli, probably right up until the name of the parish became the dominant one. The parish was named after the place of the old gatherings, where the church stood, where the priest lived and where the church organisation for a larger area was built up. By the time the assembly was moved to Bjørgvin for good, the church had gained great power in society. The large properties that in older times belonged to the temples and were heathen temple lands often became, after the change of religion, parsonage farms for the main and county churches. In addition to these properties, the farms that belonged to the small monastery that was here were also added to the parsonage, except for some on which dues had to be paid to Munkeliv Abbey in Bjørgvin. This is perhaps the explanation of why the priest here, right up to recent times, had tithes from so many farms in addition to the income from the large farm he held here in the bay by Prestesundet – the farm that gave its name to what became one of the oldest, and once perhaps also one of the largest, parishes in the country.
blocks.37: Much intriguing history is attached to Eivindvik. What I have put forward here in these “reflections” are, as mentioned, loose thoughts, but the thoughts have been created and shaped by what I have read and heard about the place, and it would be very pleasing if someone could take it as a spur to throw themselves into a study of its history.
